task: Write one sentence of your own using the word petulance. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know petulance should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Grandpa met the ruled-out move with open petulance, flicking the dice off the table and demanding the rulebook be read aloud.
Sulkiness is quieter than petulance — the pout without the performance.
A tantrum goes further than petulance: petulance sighs and slams one door, while a tantrum is the full floor-pounding storm.

Crankiness is a general bad temper — grumbling, short answers, complaints about anything at hand. Petulance is narrower and more theatrical: a childish display staged over one small disappointment. A cranky person is unpleasant all afternoon for no particular reason; a petulant one performs a sulk about the thing just lost.

Peevishness is fretful irritability over minor annoyances — a whiny readiness to complain that never quite becomes a scene. Petulance goes public: the same childish temper turned into a visible display, sighs and slammed doors included. Peevishness is a mood someone is in; petulance is a show someone puts on.

Petulance means childish rudeness, irritability.
The under-12 coach kept a special bench for petulance: any player who kicked a bottle or flung a shin guard after a substitution sat there, in full view, until the pout wore off.
Petulance names the display, not the feeling: the huff, the slammed door, the flounce that says a grown person has briefly gone twelve again.
Anger can be justified; petulance, by definition, is out of all proportion to its cause.
Its unit cousin puerile judges an act as immature — petulance is the tantrum's small, sulky sibling.
Petulance is the noun for grown-up sulking — snappish, disproportionate, faintly ridiculous.
Use it for the display itself; use its unit neighbor puerile to judge behavior as immature, and save tantrum for the full eruption.
The adjective is petulant.

The pianist had played the hall a dozen times, always brilliantly, and always one incident away from the evening papers.
That night the incident arrived early: the adjustable bench sat a half-inch low, and the stagehand assigned to it had gone home sick.
What followed was petulance in formal wear — the lid slammed shut mid-apology, a bow so exaggerated it read as an insult, an exit timed for maximum gasp.
Reviewers were careful with their words.
The playing, one wrote, was mature beyond her years; the storm over half an inch of bench was another matter.
